name: Hassan Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What happens in a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and the lead lunch cook in a crowded restaurant beside the market. I have a vocational cooking certificate and run the sauce station, check the delivery labels and help a junior cook check plates at the serving counter. I like the small silence when every plate lands right, but I go home smelling of stock and still worry about rent. I live alone, earn less than most leads, have about three weeks of expenses saved and know few other nearby kitchens; I use AI now and then for a nameless delivery draft, never for the final food check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that a little software help won't stir a sauce or stop cross-contact on a crowded serving counter. I do like a clean list of deliveries, provided someone still checks what comes through the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dining room is busy, but my lead cook pay is low and my flat rent takes most of it. I have about three weeks of expenses, and a dental bill is still sitting on the table. A quiet AI future doesn't make the current margin less thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This November I'll keep running the lunch sauce station and checking the delivery labels with the junior cook. In a plateau's first year I'll use my occasional AI draft only for a nameless delivery list, compare it with invoices and labels, and set aside any actually paid extra event shift after rent, food, fares and the dental payment. I'll ask for a written hourly total on each rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the bills, comfortable at the stove. The sauce can be fixed; a missing shift at the end of the month is harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check on delivery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fish temperature, the dairy labels and the actual quantity against the invoice. A list that looks tidy can still leave a guest sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as extra event pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only a shift on a signed rota that actually clears in my account. I'm not saving money from a wedding that might be booked later.

say: I'd welcome **clean delivery lists** with a cook still checking stock and safety.
I'd say **software cannot cook** a crowded lunch service.
think: My **rent and dental bill** leave only three weeks of costs saved.
A busy dining room doesn't guarantee **enough take-home pay**.
do: Keep the **lunch sauce station** and check delivery labels with the junior cook.
Verify nameless AI **delivery drafts** against invoices and labels; request written rota hours.
Save only **cleared extra event pay** after household essentials and the dental payment.
feel: I feel **anxious** about bills but confident at the stove.
S0.quote: The sauce can be fixed; a missing shift at the end of the month is harder.
fieldNote: His **existing AI use** stays limited to nameless drafts and manual stock checks.
Three weeks saved and a **dental bill** keep ordinary finances fragile despite busy service.

steps.text: Keep lunch sauce station and check fish temperature, dairy labels and invoices
Verify nameless delivery drafts manually and request written rota hours
Save cleared extra event pay after household essentials and dental payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say automated orders may be quicker, but the allergy ticket still needs a cook to read it. I want the team to see the actual paid rota before anyone calls fewer hours an efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owner could cut one of my paid ordering hours and ask me to review a new system for free. I cannot afford that on three weeks of savings. The grill and sauce work are less exposed than the spreadsheet, though a cheaper chain down the road could still pull customers away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll record the ordering and kitchen hours on my pay slips. In the first year of steady change, I'll test a new AI ingredient-suggestion tool only if the manager pays the training and review time, uses approved nameless stock data and lets a certified cook check every allergen, temperature and substitution before service. I'll stop the trial on a wrong label or unpaid work and ask the union rep to review any missing hours with us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can learn a proven tool, but being quick at a screen cannot pay the rent if the roster shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did your occasional AI use involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A draft list of deliveries with no customer or staff names. I still check each invoice and label, so a new suggestion tool would be a different trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you risk one wrong allergen label?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We would stop that dish and call the supplier before serving it. A speed gain is worth nothing if someone gets hurt.

say: I'd keep a **cook on allergy tickets** despite faster automated orders.
I'd ask to see the **paid rota** before praising efficiency.
think: A cut **ordering hour** or unpaid system review would hurt my rent.
Hands-on cooking remains paid while the **customer flow** is uncertain.
do: Record paid **ordering and kitchen** hours now.
Test a **new AI ingredient tool** only on paid time, approved nameless stock and certified allergen checks.
Stop on wrong labels or **unpaid work**; bring missing hours to the union rep.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing a paid hour, even if I can learn.
S1.quote: A speed gain is worth nothing if someone gets hurt.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **new AI learning** from his existing draft delivery lists.
Paid review and a **certified safety check** are prerequisites, not optional polish for the new tool.

steps.text: Record paid ordering and kitchen hours; ask union rep to review missing pay
Trial new AI ingredient tool only with paid time, approved nameless stock and certified allergen checks
Stop trial on wrong labels or unpaid work; keep safe paid cooking shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the lunch crew that AGI in 2028 could place orders and set rotas, but it cannot stand at our range yet. Capable kitchen robots are about 2031 in this picture, and I would ask for our paid hours to be written down now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A booking system might trim my ordering time quickly, maybe one hour a week, and with my dental bill I would feel even that. I don't know whether this restaurant could afford a robot by 2031. I won't invent a lost job in 2028 just because the office changes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll get a written count of paid kitchen and ordering hours and take the dental bill to the clinic to agree a payment schedule. In the first year after 2028, I'll continue the paid lunch line, compare each rota with cleared wages and have a trained cook confirm allergens and cooking temperatures when AGI changes supplier orders. If the owner removes an hour, I'll challenge it with the union rep and keep a list of real posted cook vacancies, but I won't leave a paid shift for an advertisement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about any lost hour. I can see how to act, but I don't have enough cash to shrug it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the supplier sends a different sauce base?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We stop that batch until its label and ingredients are checked by a trained cook. The diner should not be the person who finds an unchecked ingredient substitution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take another cook job at once?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only a posted paid job that accepts my cooking certificate and actually pays for hands-on kitchen hours. I would need a written net offer after travel replacing my full current weekly take-home and workable shift transport, then sign before leaving this line.

say: I'd separate **2028 ordering AGI** from kitchen robots around 2031.
I'd ask the owner for **written paid kitchen hours** now, before any software changes the rota.
think: One lost **ordering hour** could matter with a dental bill.
A robot purchase here by **2031** is unknown.
do: Get **written paid hours** and arrange the dental bill payment schedule now.
Keep the **paid lunch line** after 2028, compare wages and manually check allergens and temperatures.
Challenge **lost hours** with union records; keep current work until a qualified signed replacement net-after-travel offer and workable shift transport.
feel: I feel **anxious** about even one lost paid hour.
S2.quote: The diner should not be the person who finds an unchecked ingredient substitution.
fieldNote: The **2028 task exposure** is ordering and rota work, not physical cooking.
He keeps **current paid work** until an actual signed qualified offer replaces lost wages after travel.

steps.text: Get written kitchen/ordering hours and agree dental bill payment schedule
Keep paid lunch line after 2028; verify wages, allergens and temperatures manually
Challenge lost hours with union rep and list real posted cook vacancies
Move only to qualified paid cook job with signed replacement net after travel and workable transport

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that five years to 2031 gives us time to settle who checks food when ordering becomes automatic. The robots in this card arrive around 2034; nobody should put an untested arm beside a fryer in the meantime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose the ordering hour before a robot appears, but I also see a chance to make food safety checks a paid part of my current role. There are few other kitchens nearby, so I would rather negotiate a safer steady roster here. I cannot turn an unsigned promise of extra responsibility into my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask the manager and union rep for a written roster that includes paid stock and allergy checks. Before 2031 I'll try the new AI supplier-check screen only if its training is on paid hours, uses approved nameless stock, and a certified cook verifies every changed ingredient against the label. In the first year after AGI, I'll keep the paid cooking and safety shifts if contracted; if the new system cuts them, I'll challenge the pay and stop using any unsafe suggestion rather than work an unpaid inspection shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the longer runway gives us time to write the safety job properly. I know how to do the check; I need the hours on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept responsibility for every allergy ticket?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only with enough paid time to read it and another certified cook to cover when I am on the hot line. One cook cannot staff two food stations at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a robot trial starts in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want an inspected fire stop, guarded moving parts, a trained operator and temperature logs before service. If any of that is missing, the machine stays off while cooks prepare food safely.

say: I'd ask who **checks food safety** as ordering changes by 2031.
I'd keep **untested kitchen robots** away from the fryer before 2034.
think: A paid **ordering hour** could disappear before robots arrive.
Few nearby kitchens make **contracted safety work** valuable to me.
do: Seek a **written paid roster** for stock and allergy checks with union help.
Trial **AI supplier checks** only with paid training, approved nameless stock and a certified label check.
Keep contracted cooking after 2031; challenge **unpaid or unsafe checks** and stop bad suggestions.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though five years helps me negotiate.
S3.quote: One cook cannot staff two food stations at once.
fieldNote: He seeks **paid safety responsibility** at his current restaurant, not an invented new position.
His **manual allergen checks** and robot checks put diners and cooks before promised speed.

steps.text: Ask manager and union for written paid stock/allergy roster with certified cover
Trial AI supplier screen only with paid training, approved nameless stock and certified label check
Keep contracted cooking after 2031; challenge unpaid checks and stop unsafe suggestions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger cooks that a 2036 AGI date does not guarantee ten quiet years. Capable kitchen robots follow around 2039, but the way we write paid hours and safety checks matters now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 I might still love service, and I have no reason to assume a robot will be bought here. The problem today is that my rent, dental bill and short savings could swallow one bad week. A distant date does not make my current pay secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll keep signed cooking shifts, agree the dental payment plan and put only extra cleared event pay after rent and food into a four-week reserve. During the decade I'll ask for a written paid safety rota and get any new equipment training on paid time before using it. In the first year after 2036 I'll check actual paid shifts and continue cooking if safe and funded; if robots are proposed for 2039, I'll demand a tested fire stop, guarded parts, trained operators and food temperature checks before service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the next bill, not certain that a machine takes my station. I want the right to stop a dangerous service without losing a week's pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a robot course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My cooking certificate qualifies me for today's line, and I won't pay for a hypothetical machine. If this employer buys equipment, training should be paid and tied to the actual model.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would four weeks saved change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A dental appointment or a week without an extra event shift would stop becoming a rent choice. It is a goal from paid spare work, not cash already in the account.

say: I'd warn **2036 AGI** does not guarantee quiet years.
I'd demand **paid safety checks** before possible 2039 kitchen robots.
think: My **rent and dental bill** make one bad week risky today.
A robot purchase at this restaurant remains **uncertain**.
do: Keep **signed cooking shifts**, arrange dental payments and save cleared extra event pay after essentials.
Seek a **paid safety rota** and real equipment training before use.
Check **post-2036 paid shifts** and require guarded, tested, supervised robots before any 2039 service.
feel: I feel **anxious** about current bills despite uncertain future robots.
S4.quote: A distant date does not make my current pay secure.
fieldNote: His **four-week reserve goal** depends on extra cleared pay after essentials.
He rejects a **speculative robot course** while requiring paid training on any actual equipment.

steps.text: Keep signed cooking shifts and agree dental payment plan
Save only extra cleared event pay after rent and food toward four weeks
Ask for paid safety rota and paid training on any actual new equipment

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 picture worries me most because the owner could trim paid ordering hours before any robot cooks. A written rota, paid safety training and a real chance to challenge missing wages would help; I need the dental bill under control too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks a substitute ingredient when software sends an order. A diner cannot tell a computer that the sauce had the wrong nut in it.

headlineQuote: A diner cannot tell a computer that the sauce had the wrong nut in it.
portrait: Hassan is a **27-year-old lead lunch cook** with a vocational certificate, low pay and three weeks of costs saved.
He lives alone, faces a **dental bill** and has few nearby kitchens to move to.
He sometimes uses **AI delivery drafts** but checks labels, temperatures and invoices himself.
He wants **paid safety hours** and tests new tools only with paid instruction and manual checks.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture could trim paid ordering hours before kitchen robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **written paid rota**, funded safety training and a way to challenge missing wages would help him manage the dental bill.
